The Weight of Small Things

I keep thinking about the way my grandmother peeled an apple. One continuous spiral, the knife never leaving the fruit, the peel falling onto the newspaper she'd spread across the kitchen table. She did this every morning for my grandfather, who had diabetes and shouldn't have been eating apples at all, but he loved them, and she loved him, and so there was the apple, there was the spiral, there was the small rebellion of sweetness in a house full of careful measuring.

I was seven when I tried to do it myself. The peel broke. I cried. She didn't laugh, which I appreciated. She just took the knife and finished it, and then she let me try again with a pear, which is more forgiving, which has thinner skin, which taught me that some things are easier to learn than others.

She died in winter. I remember because the hospice nurse kept adjusting the thermostat and my mother kept adjusting it back, and they never spoke about it, this small war over degrees, over who got to decide what comfort meant. I was twenty-three. I had just started graduate school. I had just learned that my boyfriend was leaving me for someone in his program, someone who understood his work in a way I never would. I came home from the funeral and found the pear tree in my parents' backyard still holding a few fruits, brown and soft, nobody had thought to pick them.

I picked them. I made a crumble. I ate it standing at the sink, wearing my grandfather's old cardigan, which smelled like him still, like the pipe tobacco he'd quit smoking thirty years before but which somehow remained in the wool, in the closet, in the house itself.

---

There's a theory that we are all haunted. Not by ghosts, exactly, but by the versions of ourselves we used to be. The child who believed in Santa Claus. The teenager who thought heartbreak would kill her. The young adult who was certain she would change the world. These selves don't disappear. They accumulate. They sit in the back of the mind like passengers on a long train ride, occasionally leaning forward to say something, to remind you of who you were, of what you wanted, of what you lost.

I think about this when I see my students. They are so certain, so urgent, so convinced that their current crisis is the only crisis that has ever mattered. I want to tell them it gets better, but I also know that's a lie. It doesn't get better. It gets different. The crises change shape. They become quieter, more internal, less dramatic but somehow more persistent. The heartbreak doesn't kill you, but it leaves a scar. The ambition doesn't disappear, but it learns to coexist with doubt. The certainty evaporates, and in its place comes something more complicated, more honest, more useful.

I had a student last year who wrote an essay about her grandmother's hands. She described them as "map-like," full of routes and destinations and places she'd been. I gave it an A, but I wanted to give it something more. I wanted to tell her that her grandmother's hands were also young once, smooth and unmarked, that the map was written over time, that every line was a story, that she was lucky to have known the hands in their later form, when they had so much to say.

She came to office hours. She was worried about her GPA, about grad school applications, about whether she should take the job in Seattle or wait for something better. I told her about my grandmother's apple. I told her about the broken peel, the pear, the winter, the crumble eaten at the sink. She looked at me like I was speaking a foreign language. Maybe I was. Maybe that's what happens when you get older. You start speaking in stories, in metaphors, in the indirect language of people who have learned that directness rarely works, that the truth is better approached from an angle, that sometimes the most important things are the ones you almost don't say.

---

I walked past a bookstore today and saw a display of new releases. So many books. So many voices, so many attempts to make sense of the world, to capture something true, to be heard. I used to want to write a book. I still do, sometimes, in the small hours when I can't sleep and the house is quiet and I can hear my own breathing like a tide coming in and going out. But I also know now that wanting is not the same as doing. That the gap between intention and action is where most of us live, where we spend our lives, making small movements toward something we may never reach.

My mother calls every Sunday. She is eighty-two. She has started to forget things—names, appointments, the reason she walked into a room. But she remembers the apple story. She remembers the pear tree. She remembers the cardigan, the crumble, the way I stood at her sink in my grandfather's sweater and ate something sweet in a house that was already changing, already becoming the place where he would die, where she would live alone, where I would visit and try to be helpful and mostly just be present, which is its own kind of help, its own kind of love.

After we hang up, I sit with the phone in my hand. I think about all the things I didn't say. The questions I didn't ask. The silences that passed between us, comfortable and uncomfortable both, the silences of people who have known each other so long they no longer need to fill every space with words. I think about how love works this way. How it becomes a practice, a habit, a series of small attentions that accumulate into something larger than any single moment, any single conversation, any single Sunday phone call.

---

The light is changing as I write this. It's late afternoon, the time when the sun comes through the west windows and turns everything gold, temporary, precious. I think about my students again. About the essay. About the hands, map-like, full of stories. I think about my grandmother's spiral peel, unbroken, perfect, the knife moving in a circle that never ended, that could never end, that was always in the process of becoming.

I don't know what I'm trying to say. I think that's the point. Some things don't need to be said. They need to be witnessed. They need to be held in the mind like light, like warmth, like the particular quality of attention we bring to the world when we are paying attention, when we are awake, when we are here, in this moment, in this room, with these words that will disappear as soon as I stop writing them, that will remain only in the memory of having written, of having tried, of having reached toward something I may never fully grasp.

The sun is lower now. The gold is fading. I should probably make dinner. I should probably call my mother back, ask her what she had for lunch, tell her I love her, mean it, let her hear it in my voice. These are the small things. The daily practice. The spiral that continues, that must continue, that is the only immortality we have—the continuation, the next morning, the next apple, the next attempt to peel it without breaking, without crying, without needing anyone to finish what we started.

I will try again tomorrow. I will try to be worthy of the trying. I will carry the weight of all my previous selves, the child, the teenager, the young woman with her broken peel and her crumble and her cardigan, and I will move forward into whatever comes next, uncertain, hopeful, alive to the possibility that the next thing might be better, might be different, might be enough.

It is enough. It has to be. We keep going because we must, because the alternative is unthinkable, because the light is still here, still changing, still offering its temporary gold to anyone awake enough to receive it.

I am awake. I am here. I am writing.

That is all. That is everything.
